column13: We’re making slow but steady progress and recently received approval from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services to use Medicare data in our analysis.  As the full data analysis has not been undertaken yet, we have remaining funds that we are planning to commit to the analysts’ time that remain unspent.

The main reason that we lagged behind in expenditures is due to Covid-19 pandemic. For a large period of time we were not allowed to enter our laboratory. While we used the time to publish data and improve designs, we were unable to work on building instruments and other hardware. Because of this hiring had to be delayed.  
Another reason that our research was slower than expected was that a digital signal processor in our main rotating torsion balance had broken and had to be replaced with a different system. The new system had a long lead time and required new control software to be written and this software had to be debugged and tested. This activity was delayed because we were short of personnel.

In particular, we were unable to hire a postdoc to lead the effort.

We have a remaining balance of $29,000 of our $85,000 grant, which is 34% of our grant. Much of the remaining funds is in the Contract Services and travel categories. We have some outstanding expenses to pay from our Tribal Library Convening that occurred in March 2023, as well as the Beading Librarianship project. Costs that have not been paid include honorarium, catering and room costs, and travel reimbursements for at least two tribal library participants. We anticipate once the financial system is running smoothly, we will be able to close these bills. We slightly overbudgeted for participant support costs and found that some participants declined financial assistance to attend the convening. 

We were not able to make a planned trip to visit tribes in Eastern WA at the end of grant period (June 2023) due to unexpected medical issues in PI Sandy Littletree’s family. (estimated cost: $5,000). This trip is being rescheduled for August 2023. Follow-up visits to nearby tribal libraries (Squaxin Island and Nisqually) may be planned to continue the relationship building. We also plan to attend conferences during the fall quarter to disseminate results of the project. In particular, we plan to attend the Association of Tribal Archives, Libraries, and Museums conference in Oklahoma City in October.

We request a NCE for this project. The reason is delays caused by COVID. This project began in 2020 and at that time the field work (an aerial survey for polar bears in East Greenland) was canceled both in 2020 and 2021 due to COVID restrictions in Greenland. The data from that survey were a critical component of the biology portion of the project, so some of the work was paused. The survey was successfully completed this year (March-May 2023) and now we have the data to finish the final year of work under the NCE.

column41: This is a request for no-cost extension for award 2022911 “Diel growth and activity of Prochloroccocus in an Oxygen Deficient Zone”. The major goals of this project are to explore the role of the cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus in carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycling within oxygen deficient waters, focusing on samples collected from the Eastern Tropical North Pacific ODZ on a cruise funded by a previous proposal and on cyanobacterial isolates obtained from these waters on two prior cruises. This project is largely laboratory based and the COVID closure restrictions which were still in effect at UW in the fall of 2020 and most of 2021 (UW courses were taught fully online during the 2020-2021 academic year) prevented major progress on some of the aims of this work during the first year. As detailed in previous annual reports, although limited lab work was completed during this time, only limited funds were spent as well, as most personnel expenses were covered by other sources. This no-cost extension will allow a shifting of the timeline of the original proposal so activities planned for years 1-3 will be accomplished in years 2-4. I am currently on track to accomplish this COVID impacted timeline. In year 2 we completed extraction of RNA from all samples from the 2019 cruise to the ETNP (KM1920) and genetically characterized all ETNP cyanobacterial isolates in our collection which come from both 2018 and 2019 cruises, in order to focus on a subset to further characterize physiologically and genomically.  In year 3 we have selected strains for complete genome sequencing and  begun physiological experiments on a subset, focusing on the Prochlorococcus AMZII/LLVI strains. In light of the potential unusual pigment complement of our AMZII clade Prochlorococcus isolates which may possess genes for both phycobilisomes (typical Synechococcus pigments) and divinyl chlorophyll-b (typical Prochlorococcus pigments), we are performing light quality experiments (growth under blue and green wavelengths of light) and pigment composition analyses in addition to the light intensity experiments originally proposed. We are also attempting to grow one of the AMZII/LLVI and one of the LLIV strains under low oxygen conditions to measure their growth rate and transcriptional response. In the next year of the proposal (year 4, no-cost-extension year) we will complete these lab experiments and analyse the isolate genome data in comparison to metagenomes collected from the same cruises to the ETNP (these are already sequenced and were funded by a previous proposal).

column41: This grant is supporting the development and testing of an A-0-A calibrated pressure gauge on Axial Seamount.  After 3 years of testing, we recovered the instrument last summer.  Overall, the test was a success and supports the inference that A-0-A calibrations reduce drift to ~1 part in 1 million per year.  However, there were about 10 bad calibrations, mostly in the first year, which we infer are a result of blockages and possibly very slow oil leaks in the very narrow tubing in the HPLC valve used to switch the measured pressure from external to internal for calibrations.  There are significant funds left in this grant and we would like a no cost extension so that that we can use these to replace the HPLC valve with a model a wider tubing with the goal of redeploying the pressure gauge in 2024.

The reason that the award balance is over 25% of the awarded amount is due to these challenges: 

1. Team building: Finding IPC experts with the capacity to take an active role in the project has
been very challenging due to the high demand for their time in the setting of COVID, mpox, and
other emerging pathogens. Despite a lot of enthusiasm, support, and encouragement for our
project by the IPs, ID physicians, and IPC experts at our institution, they have not had the
capacity to be core members of our team. As a result, we had a delay in filling the IPC content
expert roles on our team.

2. Focus groups (IPs): The challenges facing IPs with respect to providing IPC training have been
more diverse than expected, and we have not reached thematic saturation despite conducting the
planned number of focus groups.

3. Focus groups (HCWs): Recruiting frontline healthcare workers has been much more challenging
(than recruiting IPs) due to the lack of a centralized means of contacting them. Unlike many other
professions, these workers (front desk, registration, security) tend not to be unionized or be
members of professional associations. Thus, we are reliant on leaders at the hospital helping us
identify and contact potential participants. Getting staff to sign up has been challenging, and we
have had a high no-show rate for those that have signed up.

Work will continue to develop a suite of Jupyter Notebooks for constitutive model parameter calibration and site response analysis. The notebooks will leverage existing SimCenter backend functionality (e.g. Dakota, OpenSees, etc) implemented in quoFEM and will run locally and in TACC through DesignSafe. The scope of the project included three components: i) Sensitivity analysis, ii) Bayessian parameter calibration, and iii) Uncertainty propagation to a site response analysis case. The sensitivity and parameter calibration notebooks will be customized for the PM4Sand model and will include estimation of parameters that best fit experimental data as well as their uncertainty. The site response notebook will include the uncertainties evaluated in the parameter calibration phase for the estimation of surface response for a site with liquefiable soil. This will include surface acceleration and lateral spreading. The notebooks will expand the applicability of quoFEM adding flexibility to its existing capabilities. quoFEM projects will run smoothly in these notebooks. The notebooks will complement research products developed during previous years of the project.

column13: During the past year, we surveyed the CF LTC lung transplant pulmonologists and the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) community to gather more granular details about the use of azithromycin after lung transplant. We have draft documents for many components of the Clinical Coordinating Center (MPI: Ramos and Hachem) and Data Coordinating Center (PI: Mayer-Hamblett). Scientific/Programmatic Justification for Extension: Chromosomes attach to microtubule ends via kinetochores, large multiprotein complexes that connect the DNA to the microtubule. Once attached, core kinetochore components do not turnover; however, the microtubule ends remain dynamic. The addition and removal of thousands of tubulin subunits drive kinetochore oscillations in yeast and in vertebrate somatic cells. Persistent attachment to the dynamic microtubule end is essential for accurate chromosome segregation. The attachments are mobile and robust under tension, but destabilized in response to regulatory signals that selectively cue the release of incorrect attachments. A main goal of our project is to assemble a minimal kinetochore from recombinant, purified components and measure its properties and mechanisms of regulation.  In this way, we can measure the individual contribution and regulation of each component, test models for the mechanism of assembly and error correction, and reveal unexpected properties. We assemble kinetochores on a bead by attaching nucleosomes to the bead and allowing the other kinetochore complexes to spontaneously assemble.  Then, using the optical trap, we measure the strength and/or lifetime of attachments to dynamic microtubules. We have made substantial progress on measuring the contribution of different components to the strength of attachment and to the regulation of this attachment (8 publications in the last 4 years).   However, in all our published work we have relied on nucleosomes wrapped in a DNA known to wrap nucleosomes well (“Widom 601”) instead of authentic centromere DNA sequences.  We have recently successfully wrapped nucleosomes with authentic centromeric DNA, and preliminary results show that kinetochores form stronger connections to nucleosomes wrapped in centromere DNA than to nucleosomes wrapped in 601 DNA.  In the next 12 months we will complete this dataset.   Kinetochores behave as a catch bond in that they bind more tightly to microtubules as the applied force is increased (like a finger trap).  The microtubule polymerase Stu2 is required for this behavior, but which kinetochore proteins also contribute is unknown.  We will use our kinetochore reagents to test hypotheses about which kinetochore components are required to reconstitute the catch bond behavior.

We request a no cost extension through 05/31/2025 for ONR Grant N00014-21-1-2883, Seasonal Ice Zone Reconnaissance Surveys Coordination and Ocean Profiles. This grant is for the coordination of and participation in the Seasonal Ice Zone Reconnaissance Surveys (SIZRS) program of repeated ocean, ice, and atmospheric measurements across the Beaufort Sea seasonal sea ice zone (SIZ) utilizing US Coast Guard flights of opportunity. In addition to requesting the Coast Guard flights this grant covers the conduct of hydrographic sections using primarily Aircraft Expendable CTDs (AXCTD). For, 2023 we were granted by the Coast Guard flights in June, July, August, and October. However, the scheduled flight in August suffered an engine failure soon after departing Kodiak and had to be aborted. A volcanic ash cloud generated by strong northerly winds over the Katmai Peninsula grounded the first scheduled flight in October, but the Coast Guard granted a makeup flight the following week. This was particularly critical to our AXCTD program, because of a manufacturing problem with the probes.
The AXCTDs consist of a surface float and a probe that is released by the surface float to fall through the water trailing a fine telemetry wire that sends the CTD data to the float for VHF radio telemetry to the aircraft. For 2023 we had new narrow-band AXTDs from the manufacturer (TSK) but found during the June flight that none of these would release the underwater probe from the surface float. The engineers at TSK determined that this was because of a temperature tolerance issue with the probe release hardware. Consequently, we had no working AXCTDs until TSK sent us 10 replacement probes in time for the October flight. These worked well, but we finished the 2023 season with much less AXCTD data to process than we normally have.
Partly to make up for the lack of AXCTDs, we intended to deploy ALTO profiling floats belonging to NAVOCEANO during the August flight. When that flight was aborted, we transferred the ALTO floats for deployment from USCG Healy in a cruise across the Makarov Basin. This was successful and yielded several CTD profiles in this critical region from each of three floats before the region froze over. We are presently comparing the ALTO float data to climatology from the US-Russian Atlas and finding warm Atlantic Water is intruding farther into the Makarov Basin than ever before.
Largely as a result of having less data to process, the estimated balance at the beginning of January, 2024 is $352K. The balance does not include the upcoming ONR’s final increment of $368,996. In addition, TSK will supply us about 32 new replacement narrow-band AXCTDs, which they have promised us for the 2024 season. Therefore, we ask for a no-cost extension of 15 months from 2/29/2024 to 05/31/2025. This will allow us to exploit the ALTO float and AXTD data and contribute towards support of our field activities in 2024, which we hope will include a dedicated flight to the Makarov Basin.

column17: The reasons for the request of no cost extension are as follows: (1) The start of our project was delayed because we were adjusting to changes in work plans due to the Covid-19 pandemic, especially our field work in the summer months of 2021. (2) The collection and processing of the CloudSat cloud types and radiative fluxes dataset took longer than expected. One of our key proposed research in the second year of this project is to analyze the variability of structure of the Arctic cyclones (AC)  and clouds with different cyclone types. We examined the cyclone types by using cyclone intensity and total column water vapor but came to a conclusion that alternative parameters or classification methods are preferred to more clearly define the different types of ACs.  During the rest of the project period, we plan to proceed and accomplish the following objectives: (1) Finish the AC composite type classification using both more effective physical parameters (cyclone intensity, maturity, and thermal asymmetry) and our existing k-means clustering scheme; analyze the structure of AC, cloud fraction/type/phase, and cloud radiative fluxes in different types of ACs. (2)  Use polar-WRF simulation of ThinICE cyclone cases, e.g., Aug 15-27 (cyclone #3), to examine the role of upper level cloud processes on the development of AC. (3) Prepare manuscripts for publication: (a) the characteristics and cloud structure of Arctic cyclones; (b) the role of upper level cloud processes on the development of the Arctic cyclone: a ThinICE case study.

We will need time to run our programs on a global scale to pick internal tidal beams, and to prepare/publish our database and papers. In this project, we study internal tides by resolving multiconstituent multimodal multidirectional waves in the global ocean. We have completed an internal tide database that consists of eight tidal constituents (M2, S2, N2, K2, O1, K1, P1, Q1) for the first and/or second baroclinic modes. We applied our new mapping technique to 27 years of satellite altimetry data (recently updated using 30 years of data from 1993 to 2022). We are studying the propagation and dissipation of long-range internal tidal beams, and quantifying the contributions of different decay mechanisms. This project supports a PhD student Joyce Cai at the University of Washington. We request for a non-cost extension to better finish the remaining work. It is time-consuming to do a global analysis of hundreds of long-range internal tidal beams. The student is a little slow and thus needs more time to enter a new research field.

Planning activities have been delayed for several reasons. The main issue is that we thought it prudent to gain as much information as possible from our pilot study that used multi-lung segment BALs before and 1.5 years after ETI on 9 subjects from U. Washington and U. Iowa.  This pilot study will be highly informative for future work using invasive sampling to understand ETI’s effects, the state of residual infection and inflammation in lungs of PwCF, and to understand the remaining abnormalities that have not been corrected by ETI. To maximize knowledge gained from the pilot we have used discretionary funds to markedly increase the data generated. This work includes extensive metabolomic studies on the collected BAL fluid, measurement of 96 cytokines and inflammatory assays on BAL fluid, and extensive analysis of the pre- and post- ETI CT scans using two computer /AI-driven approaches including Vida systems from U. Iowa (https://vidalung.ai/solutions/vida-discovery/) and the Therona system from Rotterdam (https://thirona.eu); as well as Brody scoring by Jason Wood’s group at U. Cincinnati. In addition we used discretionary funds to preform whole genome sequencing of 1000 Pa isolates from each patient (collected from many areas of the lung) and findings appears to be incredibly informative. We are currently analyzing these data which will inform study design and planning for the new work.   

Plan for the next year. We will continue planning activities with the group including Singh, Kappendak Goss (all UW); Ed. Mckone in Dublin; D. Stoltz in Iowa; and M. Jain at Northwestern.  We think this work and the data described above will allow us to evaluate the best approach and feasibility of a larger invasive sampling study.

Explanation of the unobligated balance.  The causes of the unobligated balance are two fold, the pandemic and a major revision of the plans for the proteomic assays.  This project started in July 2109, and during the first year of the project, the COVID-19 pandemic started. The pandemic disrupted and generally slowed down the project as many of the co-investigators and collaborators adapted and started to work from home.  When an analyst left the project, finding a replacement was difficult.

	The main cause of the delay was the change in SomaLogic’s business plan between the time the grant was submitted and the time that the application was funded. In the original application, the plan was to conduct SomaLogic assays of 1300 proteins on 3200 CHS participants who attended the 1992-93 examination, plus repeat assays on 100 participants who also attended the 1997-98 examination. These assays were to be completed by Dr. Gerszten’s lab. In the meantime, SomaLogic changed its business model with the result that outside labs such as Dr Gerszten’s lab were no longer permitted to conduct SomaLogic assays.  As a consequence, we worked with SomaLogic, the project officer for this grant, Sean Coady, and the NHLBI project officer for CHS, Phyliss Sholinsky, to develop a new assay plan. As a first step, we developed a fee-for-service contract to acquire the original set of assays described in the grant application (1300 protein assays on 3200 participants plus 100 repeats for n = 3300) in Y2 of the grant. This set of assays completed the work originally proposed in the grant application.

In conducting the assays on the original 3200 CHS participants plus 100 repeats, SomaLogic had actually used its new SomaScan version to measure 5000 proteins but only returned to CHS the subset of 1300 contracted for and paid by the grant application.  In other words, SomaLogic withheld 3700 proteins on 3300 samples.  Knowing that SomaLogic had an additional 3700 proteins on 3300 CHS samples, we undertook a series of negotiations to obtain these new data.  After some negotiations, SomaLogic and CHS agreed on a second round of assays:  if CHS purchased 7000 protein assays on an additional 500 participants at a direct cost of $625 per participant, SomaLogic would provide not only the new 7000 assays on 500 participants but also the “withheld” 3700 protein assays on the original 3200 participants plus 100 repeats at no additional cost. SomaLogic agreed to release these additional data only as part of an additional fee-for-service agreement, so our access to these data were delayed until the new 7000 assays were completed on 500 participants. Working again with the project officers for the grant and for CHS, we created a fee-for-service agreement by which these assays and data transfer would take place.

In May 2021, the CHS Steering Committee approved our request for EDTA plasma on an additional 500 CHS participants, with sampling prioritizing African-American participants not included in the original 3200. In July 2021 the fee-for-service agreement with SomaLogic was completed and CHS samples were sent to SomaLogic for assay. In late September 2021 SomaLogic returned the agreed 3700 protein measures on 3200 CHS participants, 7000 protein measures on an additional 500, and 14 SomaSignal health indicators. The total cost of these additional data was $393,750 and was paid in full in Y3 of the grant.

Planning activities have been delayed for several reasons. The main issue is that we thought it 
prudent to gain as much information as possible from our pilot study that used multi-lung segment 
BALs before and 1.5 years after ETI on 9 subjects from U. Washington and U. Iowa. This pilot study 
will be highly informative for future work using invasive sampling to understand ETI’s effects, the 
state of residual infection and inflammation in lungs of PwCF, and to understand the remaining 
abnormalities that have not been corrected by ETI. To maximize knowledge gained from the pilot we 
have used discretionary funds to markedly increase the data generated. This work includes extensive 
metabolomic studies on the collected BAL fluid, measurement of 96 cytokines and inflammatory assays 
on BAL fluid, and extensive analysis of the pre- and post- ETI CT scans using two computer 
/AI-driven approaches including Vida systems from U. Iowa 
(https://vidalung.ai/solutions/vida-discovery/) and the Therona system from Rotterdam 
(https://thirona.eu); as well as Brody scoring by Jason Wood’s group at U. Cincinnati. In addition 
we used discretionary funds to preform whole genome sequencing of 1000 Pa isolates from each 
patient (collected from many areas of the lung) and findings appears to be incredibly informative. 
We are currently analyzing these data which will inform study design and planning for the new work.
Plan for the next year. We will continue planning activities with the group including Singh, 
Kappendak Goss (all UW); Ed. Mckone in Dublin; D. Stoltz in Iowa; and M. Jain at Northwestern. We 
think this work and the data described above will allow us to evaluate the best approach and 
feasibility of a larger invasive sampling study.

Additional time beyond the established expiration date is required to ensure adequate completion of our project. 

In this project, we proposed to develop new single-cell multiomic methods for interrogating genome structure and function. The workflow of the method development consists of these ordered steps: 1) developing a protocol; 2) generating a sequencing library with the protocol; 3) small-scale NGS sequencing for method validation at the statistical level; 4) bioinformatic data analysis to validate the method;  and 5) finally, large-scale NGS sequencing for method validation, characterization, and high-quality data generation. A successful method development usually requires multiple repeating cycles of the step 1) to the step 4).  

A large portion of the award has to be budgeted to cover the cost of the large-scale NGS sequencing at the final stage. However, due to the uncertain nature of developing novel methods, the turn-around-time between the steps 3) and 5) is unexpectedly much longer than we have hoped, which lead to the remaining balance of the award is more than 25% of the awarded amount.

Technical justification:
We are requesting to extend the end date of the project titled “AUV-based Acoustic Mapping and Characterization of Seafloor Hydrothermal Discharge” from June 30th, 2024, to June 30th, 2025. This extension, once approved, will allow us to retain the remaining funds in the award for an additional year, thereby providing continued support for our ongoing research efforts. The majority of these remaining funds are designated for covering charter costs associated with conducting field testing the acoustic techniques developed as part of the project. Specifically, the initial fieldwork includes one day of at-sea experiments on R/V Nautilus during the research expedition to American Samoa, scheduled for September 2024. Further fieldwork is planned for 2025, comprising two days of at-sea experiments during a research expedition to a well-known hydrothermal vent site, such as the East Pacific Rise 9°50’N segment in February 2025. The cruise schedule is currently being finalized at the time of this request. Additionally, the remaining funds will support our research team in fieldwork reparation, as well as post-cruise synthesis and reporting.

column13: Most of our unobligated funds are at the subawards for Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium (ANTHC) and Cherokee Nation Health Service (CNHS). The delays that we incurred at ANTHC and CNHS that resulted in these unobligated funds have to do with the additional permissions that are required at these Al/ AN facilities at every step of the process to get initial approvals or approvals for modifications. For example, in addition to IRB approval and contractual agreements, ANTHC requires a concept proposal approved by the Tribal Groups involved before submitting to IRB, and then it must be divided into separate IRB proposals (i.e. Two tribal groups; South Central Foundation and ANTHC) with a total of 9 approvals required. Additional approvals of abstracts and manuscripts are required, which only occur at quarterly intervals. The delays that FHCRC and UTSW (resulting in some unobligated funds) are mostly due to downstream delays from the regulatory process at ANTHC/CNHS, because the work that occurs at FHCRC and UTSW requires specimens and/or data from ANTHC and CNHS to be performed.

column41: If the no-cost extension is approved, we anticipate continuing to make progress developing more sensitive methods for detecting mutator alleles in the BXD recombinant inbred mice, which is one of the central aims of my grant. So far, we have identified two genome-wide significant loci that affect the germline mutation rate and spectra of these mice, which are some of the first mutator alleles to be identified in a vertebrate and which have a very interesting and marked epistatic interaction with one another. However, there is suggestive evidence that several more loci may be shaping mutagenesis in these mouse strains, and we are working to increase the sensitivity of our methods in hopes of determining whether these are true biological signals. This will involve developing a polygenic framework for estimating the heritability of the mutation spectrum even when no individual locus reaches genome-wide significance. Outside of this mouse aim, we are also continuing to investigate the origins of the pulse of mutations we localized to the joint history of Europeans and South Asians. We are analyzing the linkage disequilibrium that exists between these distinctive mutations to estimate when they entered the European and South Asian populations via admixture, in hopes of determining whether this signal traces back to an ancient Anatolian population that has been identified as the "last known whereabouts" of this process.

column17: During the no-cost extension period, we will perform several projects that build upon and extend findings generated during the preceding grant period. Continuing to leverage the increasing availability of whole genome sequence data and blood cell traits, now available through additional data sets, we plan to conduct a meta-analysis of large-scale whole genome sequencing based data to investigate the genetic determinants of red blood cell traits. Results from TOPMed will be combined with results from other large-scale whole genome sequencing studies (UK Biobank, deCODE, All of Us, and a sequenced subset of the Million Veterans Program (MVP) in a meta-analysis. In each of these constituent datasets, we will run conditional analyses, adjusting for all known loci that have been reported for these traits. We plan to annotate all significant variants with information on overlap with coding regions, putative regulatory regions, as well as previously identified SNP-trait associations for these traits. To do so, we will leverage Dr. Sankaran’s recently updated variant-to-function mapping approach (SCAVENGE) which utilizes single-cell genomic data from hematopoietic cells (both single-cell chromatin accessibility (e.g., scATAC-seq) and single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to provide insights into relevant cellular context for variant-trait associations identified above. This will enable systematic mapping of regulatory elements to target genes at specific loci and with specifically mapped variants.  Finally, using the whole genome sequencing-based meta-analysis results, along with the functional annotation provided by SCAVENGE, we plan to refine our polygenic risk scores for blood cell traits in order to assess the contribution and modification of blood cell polygenic variation to blood disorder diagnoses and other complex human diseases in the UK biobank and All of Us data sets.

Our project is requesting a 1-year no cost extension due to some challenges with recruitment, which have resulted in a subsequent shift in other grant activities. So far we have recruited 41 out of 80 clinicians. 

Recruitment continues to be a challenge due to the youth mental health crisis post-COVID-19 pandemic and the associated burnout among mental health providers, which has disproportionately affected school-based clinicians. These challenges are consistent with this press release put out by NCES (see: Press Release - Over Half of Public Schools Report Staffing and Funding Limit Their Efforts to Effectively Provide Mental Health Services to Students in Need - May 9, 2024). Some other challenges we’ve encountered are complex school and agency research approval processes that create a high burden of entry, even when clinicians from the school or agency are interested and eager to participate. We have actually encountered some districts with research policies that prohibit the conduct of any research that requires student time (even 15 minutes of outside school time to simply complete behavioral health screening measures), particularly for "vulnerable" populations, which includes racial/ethnic minoritized students and/or those with physical or behavioral/mental health issues. Such policies along with regional differences in the interpretation of youth mental health consent laws (e.g., clinicians deciding that if they are not able to reach a caregiver they will not refer a youth to the study even when the youth is consenting for their own care and the study has IRB approve for a waiver of parental permission) have greatly slowed our recruitment of youth participants.

Despite these challenges, we have continued to make in-roads, building connections with agencies who provide mental health services in schools. We have established a positive relationship with New York City Department of Education and are optimistic that we will be approved to work with clinicians in the New York City Public Schools system, which is the largest public school system in the US. Recently we were approved to recruit through a mental health service agency providing school-based services in Arizona with 10 clinicians consenting to participate. We had an ambitious 2-year plan for the R34 to begin with, a third year will help us make the most of these connections we’re making and allow us to capitalize on all the work we’ve done. This no cost extension will give us the time we need to finish up our recruitment and data collection efforts as well as subsequent data analyses, interpretation, and dissemination of findings.

1)   IMPACT OF WAR ON PROGRESS: Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukraine has suffered with a magnitude that is difficult to capture in words. US officials estimate more than 500,000 casualties on both sides of the war, since February 2022. An estimated 7.5 million Ukrainians initially fled the country as refugees and 5.9 million were internally displaced, including members of the CASI-Plus study team. War crimes, including torture of prisoners, rape, and forced deportations of Ukrainian children, have been documented. The World Health Organization’s Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA) has documented 1,574 direct attacks on hospitals and clinics in Ukraine, leading to 118 deaths and 253 injuries since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine (https://extranet.who.int/ssa/Index.aspx).
 
Our collaborators / subaward partner, the Ministry of Health of Ukraine’s Public Health Center (PHC), continue to face wartime challenges. These challenges include near daily missile and bomb threats and strikes in Kyiv, the occupation of Chernihiv (one of the study sites) by Russian forces in the opening months of the war, and direct attacks at the Chernihiv Regional Hospital study site. PHC staff and study site personnel are very stretched due to displacement of the population, human resource shortages in the health sector, and escalated work demands as they pivot health services to address the needs of the Ukrainian population.
 
2)  SOFTWARE TIMELINE:  The second factor affecting the study timeline is the time to develop the CASI-Plus software tool. Exploring technology platforms that would be suitable to deploy in public-sector clinics, given Ukraine’s health regulatory environment, and that meet the design specifications for the CASI-Plus software tool took longer than planned.

Although we had a 6-month mid-term NCE in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic, our progress has been continuously and significantly impacted by the pandemic. More specifically, in the initial months during the pandemic, we had to suspend all our wet lab/bench work activities due to the Washington State governor’s “Stay Home, Stay Healthy" order. In the following months, although we were allowed to use a rotating, “skeleton crew” to conduct/maintain long-term experimentation and allowable research projects at baseline levels, our research activities were restricted due to safety measures to maintain social distancing, etc. Since then, some pandemic-related restriction policies, increased staff sick leaves, and difficulties in staff retention and hiring have continuously and significantly affected our research activities until recently. In addition to the research activities in our lab, the pandemic has also caused the suspension of any potential subject recruitment at our collaborating clinical sites.

Additionally, as we previously reported, our research activities were also affected by the closure of the Research and Training (HRT) Building that houses our lab due to a radioactive breach incident occurred in May 2019, and we were forced to relocate to a temporary lab space until the HRT building re-opened in June 2021. Therefore, some of the planned tasks in this project have been further delayed.

We request a second no-cost extension because of unanticipated research delays. At the start of the year, we had obtained a cryo-EM structure of the Mnx protein complex and submitted the result for publication. But reviewers' concerns led us to further data processing with newly released software, designed to better handle small proteins with limited symmetry and high beta sheet content such as ours. These calculations (delayed by power outages) eventually revealed a serious problem of preferred particle orientation. So we froze more grids and collected tilted cryoEM data, finally obtaining a reliable 3.5 angstrom structure that surpassed all quality checkpoints. Our paper is in the last stage of the JACS revision process.
 
We will now proceed with visualizing Mn(II) biomineralization using cryoEM under our 2023-2025 EMSL user proposal. Samples have been prepared and shipped to EMSL. Cryo-EM will define the Mnx protein conformation change, known to enable activation by Mn(II), and the location and size of nascent MnO2 particles. This structural information will complete our long-term goal of elucidating the molecular mechanism of Mn(II) biomineralization.

Justification for NSF-Approved No-Cost Extension: 
Major objectives of this project included (1) co-designing locally-contextualized digital literacy resources with and for historically marginalized communities and (2) developing infrastructure to support the extension of our co-design processes to additional communities, so that they can produce their own locally-contextualized resources. Community-based research is time intensive, and additional time is required to finalize our initial set of digital literacy resources to ensure that they are fully shareable. It is also necessary to ensure that the infrastructure we are developing is robust and capable of supporting the scaling of project processes to new communities. Finally, ensuring the sustainability of these resources and infrastructure was a goal of the project. Financial sustainability, in particular, is challenging given the core mission of providing services to historically marginalized communities. A no-cost extension is necessary to finalize sustainability planning, to ensure the project's ability to transition beyond NSF support. and is now working to create additional tools and infrastructure to support the sharing and customization of those resources at scale. 

Plan for use of unobligated funds: 
The project will use unobligated funds to complete original project objections, including finalization of digital literacy resources produced with community partners and the continued development of infrastructure (i.e., the project Web platform) to support the scaling out of the project's co-design process. Funding will also be used to test the scaling of project resources and processes to new communities, and to develop and evaluate sustainability strategies.

Staffing turnover has been a major challenge and the main cause of being unable to accomplish goals during our project period. While we hired a Prevention Educator last summer, the staff person was in her position for one month before she left the position. This position was grant funded and had significant responsibility for grant activities such as supervising a Student Advisory Group, bystander training for UW Bothell and Cascadia and ongoing prevention education for both campuses. This created delays in the implementation of the Student Advisory
Group. This position was also going to supervise a Peer Educator position which we were unable to pursue as planned. We had changes in other staff on the Violence Prevention and Advocacy (VPA) Team, with positions that weren’t grant funded and thus grant funded staff such as the Confidential Advocate had to take on additional responsibility for day-to-day operations of the VPA. Due to these staffing shortages, our department sought funding for a Peer Educator position and a Peer Education Manager professional position through student fees and successfully acquired that funding. Thus, creating a more sustainable funding structure outside of the OVW grant.
There were significant changes in staffing across both UW Bothell and Cascadia College that affected CCRT membership. We implemented a successful CCRT Co-chair model during the first year of implementation and yet staff turnover changed that during the final year. We lost Co-chair leadership and had to find replacement staff with new campus partners. This impacted our ability to evaluate the CCRT effectiveness, forge relationships with adjacent committees and create a sustainability plan.
Last fall, we ended our relationship with our community partner, LifeWire, due to a lack of involvement and an inability to agree on the scope of work. We engaged in a process of mutual agreement to end the partnership. However, we had to quickly find a new survivor serving community partner, Harborview Abuse and Trauma Center, which required a new MOU and scope of work. We had to figure out a new payment system that complied with their financial systems. During this transition, we lost an expert facilitator from LifeWire for our campus safety training. Additionally, we had challenges in securing another facilitator for campus safety training from the Washington State Coalition Against Domestic Violence due to a high demand for his services and a lack of availability in the timeframe that we needed.
The lack of staffing and capacity was the cause for not being able to organize and plan Sexual Assault Awareness month activities last spring. This has been part of our plan to offer ongoing prevention and educational opportunities throughout a student’s career at UWB and CC. Now that we are fully staffed, we have the capacity to plan for Domestic Violence Awareness Month in October. We have budget capacity for educational materials, a poster campaign and now Peer Educator positions to offer more outreach and educational programming this fall.
As for the survivor services track goal of increasing case coordination, we didn’t have adequate trust and relationship building among key stakeholders to be able to acknowledge that there was a need for improved case coordination. We also didn’t have a practical tool or ideas on next steps to be able to take. The TTI in Atlanta gave us an idea for the approach that we could use which is a Tabletop Conversation. That training showed us the gaps in our systems and how we could use the strategy of a Tabletop conversation to identify gaps and strengths in our response efforts.
The final reason for a lack of spending across the board in our budget has to do with the financial system transition that the University of Washington has been engaged in over the last year. We have worked closely with the Office of Sponsored Research to access our budget and payment systems.

column13:
Thus far we have made good progress. In the past, we successfully collected survey data from a sample of people experiencing homelessness in the Seattle area. We also collected survey data from people in housing, the general population. As we planned with our first no-cost extension, we are working to collect a mail-out survey that will test our ability to contact and solicit responses from the general population, including the difficult step of randomly selecting one person from the household to participate in the survey. Our goal with this plan is to create a process that will provide high response rates and reduce selection bias, which we can then apply to funded survey projects in the future. Indeed, some of these projects are already planned, and we detail them below.

The mail-out test survey is taking longer than we originally planned. This is because we had planned on using a survey organization (CHRR) at The Ohio State University to program our complex questionnaire with random selection of household members. They originally agreed to do this at low cost, given the pilot nature of our study, however, they have since indicated that they are not willing to help us with the programming. As such, we have taken this task on ourselves. Because we already have future projects in the planning and contracting stage (which I will explain more below), we decided to take on the full complex programming in REDCap software, instead of a simpler and quicker questionnaire programming software. Designing all our complexity into REDCap sets us up well for future projects, but it has taken much longer than expected. That said, we are in the final stages of programming and testing and expect to begin the mail-out survey in the next couple of weeks. As a side note, we have also engaged an undergraduate research assistant in this task and she has proven exceptionally skillful and has learned much about survey methods and sociology in the process.
Unforeseen delays in FDA approval delayed the project.
